## The problem
<!-- 
  Describe the issue you are experiencing here to communicate to the
  maintainers. Tell us what you were trying to do and what happened.
-->
All my input_datetimes are in UTC and not my local time zone. I went back to 0.117.6 and the timestamp is handled correctly. I opened #43186 but I do not think I described the issue properly and it was closed.

For an input_datetime set to today's date at 6 AM

**0.117.6**
`{{state_attr('input_datetime.heater_time_variable','timestamp') | int | timestamp_custom ('%H:%M', False)}}`
That template generates 11:00 (which is the correct UTC time)

`{{state_attr('input_datetime.heater_time_variable','timestamp') | int | timestamp_custom ('%H:%M', True)}}`
That template generates 6:00 (which is the correct local time)

**0.118b3**
`{{state_attr('input_datetime.heater_time_variable','timestamp') | int | timestamp_custom ('%H:%M', False)}}`
That template generates 6:00 (which is the incorrect UTC time)

`{{state_attr('input_datetime.heater_time_variable','timestamp') | int | timestamp_custom ('%H:%M', True)}}`
That template generates 1:00 (which is the incorrect local time)

`{{ utcnow().tzinfo }}` - generates the correct information
`{{ now().tzinfo }}` - generates the correct information
`sensor.time`shows the correct information

I restarted the host machine a couple times which did not resolve the issue.

  and find the issue quicker. Version information is found in the

-->

- Link to integration documentation on our website: https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/input_datetime/

-->

```yaml

```

I just upgraded my test system to the release version of 0.118. The template test I had suggested (above) does not produce the same result as it did in 0.117.

The template based on the input_datetime's timestamp now reports:
```
2020-11-16 08:14:00
```
The displayed time is 5 hours _earlier_ than the actual time displayed by the input_datetime. This 5-hour discrepancy corresponds to the offset between local time and UTC.

The timestamp-based template maintains a 5-hour offset regardless if the input_datetime is changed via a service call or via the UI.

This 'offset' behavior is definitely something new (and undesirable) in 0.118.

More test results:

If the input_datetime only handles time, not date, the template reports the same results in both 0.117.5 and 0.118.0.  

In other words, if the time is `12:00:00`, the template reports `1970-01-01 07:00:00`.

If you replace `timestamp_local()` with `timestamp_utc()`, the template will report `1970-01-01 12:00:00`. What this implies is that the time entered by the user is assumed to be in UTC, not local, and so the timestamp is created _without any compensation for timezone offset_. Naturally, if you then employ `timestamp_local()` (as one normally does when converting Home Assistant's UTC-based timestamps) it proceeds to compensate for an offset that was _never originally applied to the timestamp_.

I think the problem is that there may be inconsistencies in how an input_datetime's timestamp is computed depending on whether it handles time and date or just time or just date. I believe the UTC time recorded in its timestamp should be a conversion from local to UTC time. Most users who define a time, in an input_datetime, are entering a _local_ time, not a UTC time, so the timestamp should incorporate the conversion.

> And that's expected and correct?

I'm compelled to say that I think it's incorrect. All timestamps in Home Assistant are UTC time yet this one instance _deviates from the norm_. It's effectively storing the time as a _local_ timestamp (not UTC).

If I use an input_datetime to store an alarm time such as `2020-11-20 08:30` or just `08:30`, both represent my _local_ time. That means they must be converted to UTC in order to create a UTC timestamp. To get local time from the timestamp, one can simply use `timestamp_local()` (as with any of Home Assistant's timestamps).

However, that's not how it currently works with a time-only input_datetime. It performs no conversion to UTC therefore its timestamp is _local_ time. It means that if one wants to get local time from its timestamp, one must (counter-intuitively) use `timestamp_utc()`.

Sure, we could document this anomaly ("All timestamps are UTC with one notable exception ...") but why not just make it work like everything else does?
Timestamps only work for datetimes. Dates don't have times and mean the same regardless of timezones. The same with times.

> Timestamps only work for datetimes.

Which is why time is currently encoded as a timestamp by adding the "Unix Epoch": `1970-01-01`. The problem is it overlooks to first convert the local time to UTC.

If my input_datetime is set to `08:30` (EST) it should be adding 5 hours to that and then encoding `1970-01-01 13:30` as a timestamp. However, it doesn't; it encodes `1970-01-01 08:30`. That makes it an exception to how all other timestamps are encoded (as UTC time).

This mistake used to be limited to a time-only input_datetime but now, in 0.118, it's also doing it for a time&date input_datetime.

I figure if there's a fix being implemented it ought to apply to both types of input_datetime (time&date and time-only).

> Timestamps only work for datetimes.

For clarity, I believe this was meant to be "_Timezones_ only work for datetimes."

> The problem is it overlooks to first convert the local time to UTC.

Converting between local time and UTC without having a date is futile. You will get random errors due to time shifts around daylight saving time (DST). Timezones also do change occasionally so the offset could be different in different years. This means that just using 1970 leaves one with a value that is all but useless.

Probably the right thing would be to remove `timestamp` from time-only entities but I guess a reasonable compromise that is still useful would be to recalculate for the current date at each midnight (local time).
